acceleration.d: Carrying out the planned scope in less time than anticipated, or an increased scope within the original duration. Usually costs more per unit of work than normal working, because overtime, extra shifts and additional crews are all less efficient than the plan they replace.

abcp.d: The chain of activities that actually determined when the project finished, **deduced** from records rather than calculated by software. Float values only run forward of a data date, so no package can compute this for you.

asbuilt.d: A record of what actually happened: start and finish dates for every activity, and — done properly — the periods of inactivity between spells of real progress.

asplanned.d: The contractor's intentions before any work started. Also called the baseline. It is a statement of intent, not a record of fact, and it is the base from which change is measured.

alv.d: The delay or recovery attributable to one activity, measured **net** of all variance that came before it. Without the netting, every activity downstream of a late one looks late too.

additive.d: Any method that inserts delay events into a programme and recalculates. The cause is known; the effect is projected. Impacted as-planned and time impact analysis are both additive.

aoa.d: The original diagramming method, where the arrow is the activity and the node is an event. Every relationship was finish-to-start, which made the critical path obvious. No current software supports it.

aon.d: The precedence diagramming method: the box is the activity, the arrow is the relationship. More flexible than activity-on-arrow, and far less intuitive to read — which is the trade.

backward.d: Working from the end of the network to the start, calculating the latest each activity can start and finish without delaying completion. Produces late start and late finish.

baseline.d: The agreed as-planned programme. It is not affected by actual progress — only by a deliberate, documented change of intention for the remaining work.

bcwp.d: The earned value: the budget for the work actually completed. Compare with BCWS for schedule performance, with ACWP for cost performance.

bcws.d: The planned value: the budget for the work that should have been done by now.

acwp.d: What has actually been spent to date.

cab.d: A subtractive method. Take the as-built programme, remove the delay events, and see when the project would have finished but for them. Its weakness is that as-built logic has to be invented before anything can be collapsed.

casual.d: The link from an event to its effect. Liability comes from the contract; causation comes from the facts. Delay analysis exists to satisfy causation in a way that lets damages be assessed.

ccm.d: A derivative of the theory of constraints. Uses average durations, calculates backwards from the required date, and pools contingency into explicit buffers rather than padding individual activities.

compensable.d: A critical delay caused by an employer risk event that the contract makes recoverable in money. Time and money are separate tests — passing one does not pass the other.

concurrency.d: Two or more effective causes of delay of equal causative potency, one at the employer's risk and one at the contractor's, whose effects are felt over the same period. True concurrency — same start, same end — is rare; concurrent *effect* is common.

constraint.d: A date imposed on an activity that overrides or supplements the network logic. Useful in moderation. Over-used, it prevents the programme from calculating a sensible critical path at all.

constructive.d: Where an employer fails to recognise a valid entitlement to time, and the contractor is forced to accelerate to avoid liquidated damages. A US doctrine, argued elsewhere with varying success.

cpi.d: BCWP ÷ ACWP. Below 1.00 means the work completed has cost more than budgeted — and statistically, once CPI drops below 1 it very rarely recovers.

cpm.d: A mathematical model built on two variables — activity durations and activity relationships — that determines the shortest time a project can be completed in, which activities determine it, and how much slack everything else has.

cre.d: An event which, under the contract, is not at the employer's risk. When it causes delay it becomes a contractor delay event (CDE). Anything unexplained defaults here.

critical.d: The sequence of activities whose durations determine the overall project duration. There can be more than one, and it moves. Strictly it is the path with the **least** float, which on a late project is the most negative.

culpable.d: Delay caused by the contractor's own act or omission, or otherwise at its risk under the contract.

datadate.d: The date up to which progress has been recorded and from which all remaining work is re-scheduled. Everything left of it is history; everything right of it is a forecast.

dominant.d: The approach that asks which of several competing causes was the effective or predominant one. Given early judicial support, later doubted, and never quite dead. It is relevant to recovering damages, not to relief from them.

disruption.d: Interference with the flow, continuity or sequence of planned work, producing lower efficiency. Unlike delay, it always has a direct financial consequence — and it can occur on a project that finishes on time.

driving.d: The predecessor link that actually set a successor's early start. When an activity has several predecessors, only the one that determined the date is driving — and only driving links carry the critical path.

eot.d: Relief from liquidated damages, and a new completion date. Its benefit to the employer is preserving the right to deduct damages at all — without it, time can become at large.

ere.d: An event which, under the contract or by later determination, is at the employer's risk. When it causes delay it becomes an employer delay event (EDE).

earlycomp.d: A programme showing an intention to finish before the contract date, creating terminal float. Submitting one does not change either party's contractual rights, and does not oblige the employer to release information any earlier.

excusable.d: A delay caused by an employer risk event, which relieves the contractor from damages. Whether it also carries money is a separate question entirely.

efloat.d: How long an activity can be delayed without moving the early start of any successor. Spend it and you take contingency from the next trade, not from the project.

float.d: Time available to an activity over and above its planned duration. A relative measure of which activities are more critical than others — and a value that can be manufactured by calendars, constraints and calculation settings.

forward.d: Working from the start of the network to the end, calculating the earliest each activity can start and finish. Produces early start, early finish, and the shortest possible project duration.

fragnet.d: A small sub-network of activities representing one delay event, inserted into a base programme complete with its own durations, predecessors and successors.

gantt.d: A time-scaled bar chart. Excellent at showing what happens when; incapable, without logic, of showing what is critical or what a change would do.

global.d: A claim for the total overrun or total cost overspend, without a discrete causal link between each event relied on and each element of loss. Permitted in narrow circumstances, and very hard to sustain.

iap.d: The simplest CPM-based method: insert employer events into the baseline and see where completion moves. Theoretical by construction, since it assumes everything else went to plan.

interfering.d: Float which, if used, reduces the float available to successors. It is the difference between total and free float, viewed from the other side.

independent.d: Time an activity can absorb without affecting either its successors' early starts or its predecessors' late finishes. Always less than or equal to free float.

jbr.d: A workshop with designers, engineers, estimators, the client and the trades to test the assumptions and constraints behind a draft programme before it is fixed as the baseline.

lag.d: Time imposed between two activities in a relationship. Positive lag delays the successor; negative lag lets it start earlier than the logic would otherwise allow, and is almost never defensible.

ld.d: A pre-agreed rate payable by the contractor for late completion. The purpose of an extension of time, from the contractor's side, is relief from these.

longest.d: The chain of driving relationships back from project completion. Not identical to 'least float': constraints can give an activity terrible float without it driving anything.

measuredmile.d: Compare productivity in a period unaffected by disruption with the same or similar work in a disrupted period, and claim the difference. Favoured by the courts because it uses the project's own data — and utterly dependent on which period you choose.

milestone.d: A zero-duration activity marking the start, interface or completion of a defined scope. It has no work in it, which is why it takes its date from its last predecessor.

mitigation.d: Reasonable steps to reduce the effect of a delay or disruption. It is not the same as acceleration, and a contractor is not generally required to spend money to mitigate somebody else's delay.

negfloat.d: The earliest an activity can start is later than the latest it should have started. A measure of how far behind programme a path is — and a value that constraints can manufacture out of nothing.

neutral.d: Excusable but non-compensable: time but no money. Exceptionally adverse weather and force majeure are the usual examples, and both need defining in the contract to avoid argument.

override.d: A calculation setting that breaks the link between an activity and its predecessors when it starts out of sequence. It will happily report an impossible sequence and a completion date nobody has earned.

pacing.d: Deliberately slowing work in the knowledge that a more critical delay is happening elsewhere, to avoid spending money on progress that would only wait. Arguable only on four limbs of contemporaneous evidence.

pert.d: Programme Evaluation and Review Technique. Uses three durations per activity — optimistic, most likely and pessimistic — to give a distribution of completion dates instead of one date. Useful where there is no historic data; of little use forensically.

prolongation.d: Time-related cost incurred because the works ran longer. Recoverable only for time actually taken and loss actually suffered — not by applying an average rate to a theoretical period.

retained.d: A calculation setting that keeps a dependency even when the successor starts out of sequence. The honest option: work may start early, but it cannot be complete until its predecessor is.

rpfsa.d: AACE International's Recommended Practice on Forensic Schedule Analysis, issued 2007. Technical rather than contractual, aimed squarely at reducing subjectivity, and the source of the method implementation protocol taxonomy.

scl.d: The Society of Construction Law Delay and Disruption Protocol, first published October 2002. Twenty-one core principles aimed at dispute avoidance. Guidance, expressly not a statement of law.

spi.d: BCWP ÷ BCWS. Below 1.00 means less value has been earned than planned. It measures schedule in money, so it cannot tell you which activities are late — only that something is.

sequester.d: Hiding available float so a programme appears more critical than it is: padded durations, preferential logic, excessive lags, or a zero-total-float constraint. Expressly prohibited in many US specifications.

subtractive.d: Any method that removes delay events from an as-built programme to find when completion would otherwise have occurred. Collapsed as-built is the only common example.

terminal.d: The gap between planned completion and the contract completion date. Every argument about who owns the float is really an argument about this.

tia.d: Additive, multiple-base. Progress is entered up to the day before each event, the fragnet goes into that programme, and the movement is recorded. The SCL Protocol's preferred technique for deciding entitlement at the time.

totalfloat.d: How long an activity can be delayed without moving project completion. Late finish minus early finish, or late start minus early start — the two are always the same number.

timerisk.d: Contingency built into an activity's own duration. Legitimate, but better declared explicitly than buried — buried contingency is indistinguishable from an inflated duration, and Parkinson's Law will consume it either way.

watershed.d: A windows analysis where the windows are set by significant milestones rather than by the calendar. Useful when the nature of the work changes — design to construction, construction to commissioning.

wbs.d: A hierarchical decomposition of the whole project into elements, coded so that cost and programme can be reported against the same structure. Too shallow and it hides overruns; too deep and it becomes unmanageable.

windows.d: Not a technique in itself — simply the period being analysed. Any of the primary methods can be run in windows, and doing so is usually an improvement on running it across the whole project at once.

wlv.d: Delay measured at the end of each window rather than against each activity. Coarser than activity level variance, and less able to identify concurrency.
